entry.title: Mishra and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2327
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Mishra’s Subclass 155 Five-Year Resident Return visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Mr Mishra accepted he did not pass the character test because of a 22-month aggregate sentence for family violence offences. The Tribunal affirmed the non-revocation decision after considering whether another reason existed under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii) and Direction No. 110.

Key holding: Where a visa is mandatorily cancelled because the holder fails the character test due to a substantial criminal record, the Tribunal must consider whether there is another reason to revoke under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), applying Direction No. 110.

In accordance with s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), the Tribunal must therefore consider whether there is another reason to exercise the discretion under s 501CA(4) to revoke the original decision.

entry.title: Onyema v Commonwealth of Australia (as represented by the Australian Taxation Office) (extension of time, application for stay) [2026] FCA 1530
entry.content:
Kenneth Onyema sought judicial review of the ATO’s decision to terminate his APS employment for unauthorised access to taxation records. In this interlocutory judgment, the Federal Court held that he did not need an extension of time, refused a stay of the termination decision, granted leave to amend, and fixed the proper respondents.

Key holding: Under s 11(1)(c) of the ADJR Act, an application for review is “lodged” when it comes into the possession of the Registry or its staff, not when it is later accepted and filed, so receipt within the prescribed period satisfies the time limit.

An application for review will be "lodged" when it comes into the possession of a Registry or a staff of a Registry: EIW20 at [67], quoting Hong v Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs [1998] FCA 341; (1998) 82 FCR 468 at 471 (the Court).

entry.title: Lye v Comcare [2026] FCA 1517
entry.content:
This was a Federal Court appeal from an Administrative Review Tribunal decision concerning weekly compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). The Tribunal had equated Mr Lye’s capacity to work full-time usual hours in administrative duties with an ability to earn his normal weekly earnings, reducing compensation to zero. The Court found legal error and, by consent, set aside the decision and remitted the matter for redetermination.

Key holding: Under s 19(2) of the SRC Act, the Tribunal must separately assess the amount per week the employee is able to earn in suitable employment and use that to determine the reduction to NWE; merely equating capacity for normal hours with NWE is legal error.

In its reasons at [40], the Tribunal failed to address the amount per week (if any) that the applicant was able to earn in suitable employment during the relevant periods (i.e., the fourth question). As a result of the above failure, the Tribunal failed properly to address the amount (if any) by which the applicant's NWE should be reduced in order to determine the amount of compensation that he is entitled to receive (i.e., the sixth question).

entry.title: Mohamedali v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1531
entry.content:
The Federal Court allowed a consent judicial review application concerning a decision by the Assistant Minister under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to cancel the applicant’s visa. The Assistant Minister conceded jurisdictional error because he failed to consider an updated psychologist’s report that was constructively before him and relevant to the applicant’s risk of reoffending. The Court made orders quashing the cancellation decision.

Key holding: A s 501BA decision is affected by jurisdictional error if the Minister fails to properly consider material constructively before him that is relevant to the risk the applicant poses to the Australian community and the national interest.

Accordingly, the Assistant Minister accepts that his decision was affected by jurisdictional error as a result of his failure to properly consider the risk the applicant posed to the Australian community.

entry.title: AQP23 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1521
entry.content:
AQP23 appealed from the Federal Circuit and Family Court, which had dismissed judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of her protection visa under s 109 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) for incorrect answers about citizenship. On appeal to the Federal Court, she argued the Tribunal’s hijab-related harm finding was legally unreasonable and that it failed to consider lesser “non-PV” harm. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal with costs.

Key holding: A tribunal is not required to expressly engage with claims about lesser forms of harm that the applicant has not clearly made.

It could scarcely be said that the Tribunal was required to expressly engage with claims about lesser forms of harm, including the "hijab sanction" and "non-PV harm", when the appellant never made claims clearly expressed in such terms

entry.title: Smith v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1520
entry.content:
Mr Smith, a New Zealand citizen, had his Class TY Subclass 444 visa cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after criminal convictions and imprisonment. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed that refusal. On judicial review, the Federal Court found the Tribunal misconstrued Direction 110’s definition of “family violence” and set aside its decision.

Key holding: Conduct falling within an example of family violence in Direction 110 cl 4 is not automatically family violence; it must also have the effect of coercing or controlling a family member or causing that person to be fearful.

For example, behaviour which involves "intentionally damaging or destroying property" will not necessarily constitute family violence. It will only do so if that behaviour had the effect of coercing or controlling a member of the perpetrator's family, or causing the family member or members to be fearful.

entry.title: Gautama v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1519
entry.content:
The applicant sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of his cancelled Five-Year Resident Return (Class BB) (Subclass 155) visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). He argued the Tribunal erred by failing to apply the s 201 “10-year rule”, failing to consider mandatory considerations and misconstruing s 501CA(4)(b)(ii) as discretionary. The Federal Court dismissed the application.

Key holding: Section 201 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), the “10-year rule”, has no application to mandatory visa cancellation under s 501(3A), because s 201 belongs to the separate deportation framework.

I accept the Minister's submissions. The Tribunal was correct in its conclusion that s 201 had no application to the matter before it.

entry.title: Papa v Commissioner of Police [2026] NSWSC 1263
entry.content:
The plaintiff sought judicial review of decisions revoking his Category AB firearms licence, including the original revocation and an internal review affirming it. The Supreme Court held only the internal review decision was operative and reviewable, found no failure to consider mandatory considerations or legal unreasonableness, and dismissed the summons.

Key holding: Where an original administrative decision is affirmed on internal review under s 53 of the ADR Act 1997 (NSW), only the review decision is legally operative and amenable to judicial review.

That conclusion, which was essentially argued by the defendant, means that, in the present circumstances, the second is the operative decision. It is only that decision which is amenable to judicial review.

entry.title: Younes v Younes (No 2) [2026] NSWSC 1261
entry.content:
Lolita Younes sought declaratory relief and specific performance concerning agreements relating to the subdivision/sale of the front block at 36 Page Street, Wentworthville. The substantive claim and Susie Younes’s cross-claim were dismissed by consent after subdivision and transfer to Lolita were completed. Stern J determined the reserved costs issue on the papers and made no order as to costs.

Key holding: Where proceedings are dismissed by consent without a merits determination, the court may make no order as to costs if it cannot conclude any party acted unreasonably or would have succeeded on the merits.

In these circumstances I am not satisfied that any one party has acted unreasonably in commencing or defending proceedings or that any one party would have been successful had the various claims been determined on their merits. Having regard to this, the appropriate order is that there be no order as to the costs of the proceedings

entry.title: CYZGC by his plan nominee and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2332
entry.content:
The applicant, a 10-year-old NDIS participant, sought interim relief after a reassessment increased his core supports but reduced his therapy funding and added behaviour support. He asked the Tribunal under s 32(2) of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth) to reallocate or make flexible the behaviour support funding, or alternatively to stay Plan-2 so Plan-1 revived. The Tribunal refused, finding neither order desirable to ensure the effectiveness of the review, and recommended an early conference and hearing.

Key holding: Under s 32(2) of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth), an interim stay or other order is made only if desirable to ensure the effectiveness of the review; hardship, even serious hardship, is insufficient unless it puts the effectiveness of the review in jeopardy.

Finally, in relation to hardship, it is not enough that the decision causes hardship, even serious hardship. The discretion may only be exercised where the degree of hardship is such that it puts the effectiveness of the review in jeopardy.[5]

entry.title: CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency and NGVL (Guidance and Appeals Panel) [2026] ARTA 2328
entry.content:
The Guidance and Appeals Panel reviewed an ART decision that had found funding for an Orangutan Plus Funky Monkey Bars Frame and accessories to be a reasonable and necessary NDIS support for NGVL, a child with Autism and ADHD. The Panel focused on whether the equipment was “standard indoor or outdoor play equipment” excluded by item 4(p) of Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules.

Key holding: Standard outdoor play equipment falling within item 4(p) of Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules is not an NDIS support and cannot be funded unless it is modified or adapted to address the participant’s functional impairments.

For the reasons given below, the Panel concludes that the Funky Monkey Bars Frame and accessories are 'standard...outdoor play equipment' and are therefore an excluded support under item 4(p) in Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules. On this basis it cannot be included for funding in NGVL's SOPS.

entry.title: LFQR and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security second review) [2026] ARTA 2320
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a refusal to pay family tax benefit top ups and supplements for 2022/23 because the applicant’s partner lodged his income tax return on 4 July 2024, after the 30 June 2024 reconciliation deadline. The applicant relied on stress, family violence, alcohol issues, a brief separation and pandemic-related pressures. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding no special circumstances that prevented the partner from lodging on time.

Key holding: Under s 32D(1)(c)(ii) of the Administration Act, special circumstances will only extend the reconciliation time if they actually prevented the partner from lodging the income tax return by the required date.

For the Applicant to be paid top ups and supplements of family tax benefit for 2022/23, the Tribunal must be satisfied that there are special circumstances that prevented the Applicant's partner from lodging his income tax return by 30 June 2024.

entry.title: Morton v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] HCA 38
entry.content:
The High Court dismissed Gary Gerard Morton's application for constitutional writs challenging a delegate's refusal of a Return (Residence) (Class BB) visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Morton alleged the delegate failed to consider his claims about access to HIV, mental health and sobriety supports in Singapore and made legally unreasonable risk findings. The Court found no jurisdictional error, granted a short extension of time and dismissed the application with costs.

Key holding: A decision-maker is not required to give reasons by reference to every separate provision of Direction 110 or to repeat, in each relevant paragraph, the evaluation of information considered elsewhere.

Nothing in Direction 110 or s 501G(1) of the Migration Act requires a decision-maker to give reasons for their decision in a form which sets out the totality of the decision-maker's reasons by reference to each separate provision of Direction 110 including every piece of information evaluated and every finding of fact relevant to the decision-maker's assigning of weight to the specified matter which the provision requires the decision-maker to consider.

entry.title: Jaworski v Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand (No 2) [2026] NSWCA 213
entry.content:
Mr Jaworski sought to set aside or vary the Court of Appeal’s earlier leave judgment under UCPR r 36.16, and CA ANZ sought gross sum costs. The Court dismissed the reopening application and fixed costs at $30,000 for the leave/recusal application and $6,000 for CA ANZ’s notice of motion. The dispute concerned alleged errors, bias/prejudgment and costs in ongoing litigation involving CA ANZ.

Key holding: Under UCPR r 36.16, reopening requires some error in the court's reasoning due to misapprehension of fact or law that is not solely attributable to the applicant's neglect or default.

What is required to be established on an application under r 36.16 is some error in the court's reasoning because of a misapprehension of the facts or misapprehension of the relevant law; and that this misapprehension cannot be attributed solely to the neglect or default of the party seeking the rehearing.

entry.title: Hui and Commissioner of Taxation (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2319
entry.content:
The applicant sought review of several Taxation Office decisions concerning his income tax affairs, including invalid objection determinations. The Tribunal found it had no jurisdiction because the decisions were not reviewable objection decisions under s 14ZQ of the Taxation Administration Act 1953 (Cth). The application was dismissed.

Key holding: A decision that is not a reviewable objection decision within s 14ZQ of the Taxation Administration Act 1953 (Cth) is not reviewable by the Tribunal under s 14ZZA, so the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction.

I have had due regard to the decisions submitted by the applicant and find that they are not reviewable objection decisions within the meaning of section 14ZQ of the Taxation Administration Act 1953 (Cth) and, accordingly, the Tribunal has no jurisdiction under section 14ZZA to review them.

entry.title: Coe and Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority [2026] ARTA 2317
entry.content:
Jason Coe applied to have Jardini Pty Ltd’s Great Barrier Reef Marine Park permit transferred to him personally. The Authority refused, and on review the Tribunal found he was a suitable person but still affirmed refusal because other matters under s 120(c) of the GBRMP Regulations concerned the objects of the GBRMP Act and orderly management of the Marine Park. The Tribunal also resolved procedural issues about production, redactions and deciding on the papers.

Key holding: Even where the Tribunal does not find a proposed transferee unsuitable, it may refuse transfer under s 120(c) because of other matters relevant to the objects of the GBRMP Act or management of the Marine Park.

For the reasons set out in more detail below, the Tribunal has not found the Applicant to be an unsuitable person. However it does believe that at this time, and having regard to the present circumstances, there are matters which are relevant to the proposed transfer and the objects of the GBRMP Act and management of the Marine Park such that the transfer of the Permit should not be approved.

entry.title: Kay and Commissioner of Taxation (Taxation and business) [2026] ARTA 2310
entry.content:
Matthew Kay objected to superannuation guarantee charge assessments for failing to make superannuation contributions for Daryl Marschke for 1 July 2019 to 30 June 2023. The Commissioner initially found Mr Marschke was not an employee but later reversed that position on delegation issues and assessed SGC. The Tribunal affirmed the objection decision.

Key holding: A contract is not wholly or principally for a person’s labour if it leaves the contractor free to do the work personally or employ others, even if the contractor in fact performs most of the work.

Even where a person has performed the bulk of the work under the contract, or it was the expectation of the parties that the person would do so, a contract that 'leaves the contractor free to do the work himself or employ other persons to carry it out' is not wholly or principally for the labour of the person.

entry.title: South Australian Commission for Catholic Schools Inc and Secretary, Department of Education (Guidance and Appeals Panel) [2026] ARTA 2304
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed 2024 Commonwealth recurrent funding determinations for 84 non-government Catholic schools in South Australia. It unanimously held that mid-year reception students who began in term 3 2024 were “primary students” because reception was the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1. A majority then held those students did not have a pattern of regular attendance at school or school generally during 2024, so they failed reg 9B(1)(c) and were ineligible unless the Minister included them under reg 9B(3).

Key holding: Reception undertaken by mid-year reception students is the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1, so those students are primary students in that calendar year.

Giving the phrases to which I have already referred their natural meaning, the logical conclusion is that the 2024 mid-year reception students were in the year of schooling in a course of primary education that was immediately before year 1. entry.title: Mr Mark Shorrock v Cinc Switchboards Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3911
entry.content:
Mark Shorrock made a s.365 general protections application against Cinc Switchboards Pty Ltd, alleging constructive dismissal. The Commission determined a jurisdictional objection that he had resigned voluntarily and was not dismissed. It upheld the objection and dismissed the application.

Key holding: A resignation is a dismissal under s.386(1)(b) only where the employer’s conduct or course of conduct was intended to bring about the resignation or had the probable result that the employee had no effective or real choice but to resign, with employer conduct being essential.

To satisfy the test for constructive dismissal requires a substantive and demonstratable course of conduct aimed at bringing about the end of the employment. This action is evident in the actions of the Employer, and the intended result of the conduct to bring about the Applicant's resignation; or that that would be the probable result.

entry.title: Mrs Karen Brown v St John of God [2026] FWC 3894
entry.content:
Karen Brown lodged an unfair dismissal application under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) after her dismissal on 29 July 2026, but the application was lodged on 22 August 2026, outside the 21-day period. The Fair Work Commission considered whether to extend time, found no exceptional circumstances, and dismissed the application. The case is a straightforward extension-of-time decision.

Key holding: An unfair dismissal application lodged out of time can only proceed if the Commission is satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist, assessed by the s 394(3) factors.

The Commission can only extend time if it is satisfied that there are 'exceptional circumstances', taking into account the matters in ss 394(3)(a) to (f).

entry.title: Ms Alex Culhane v Psychsense Therapeutic Services Pty Ltd & Chantelle Chapman [2026] FWC 3893
entry.content:
Ms Culhane applied under s.365 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), alleging dismissal by Psychsense Therapeutic Service Pty Ltd and Ms Chapman. The Commission had to determine a jurisdictional objection that she had not been dismissed because she resigned. Deputy President Clancy found there was no dismissal and dismissed the application.

Key holding: For a s.365 application at the material time, the Commission lacks jurisdiction unless the applicant was actually dismissed under s.386(1), meaning termination on the employer’s initiative or a resignation forced by employer conduct.

I have concluded that in this case there was no dismissal within the meaning of s.386 of the Act because I am satisfied there was no termination of the Applicant's employment on the Respondent's initiative and nor have I been persuaded that the Applicant was forced to resign because of conduct or a course of conduct engaged in by the Respondent .

entry.title: Costantino v Hillier (No 2) [2026] NSWSC 1260
entry.content:
This is a costs decision following the Court’s earlier determination of limitations issues in a professional negligence claim. The plaintiff failed to obtain an extension of the long-stop limitation period for claims concerning the first four surgeries, while the defendant’s separate question also affected claims concerning the fifth and sixth surgeries. The Court ordered the costs of the plaintiff’s notice of motion and the separate question to be costs in the cause, rather than acceding to the defendant’s proposed 75% costs order.

Key holding: Where parties achieve mixed success on overlapping interlocutory limitation applications, the Court may exercise its costs discretion by ordering costs in the cause rather than apportioning costs issue-by-issue.

In my view, the parties have each achieved some success and some failure in their competing applications which were heard before me on 18 and 19 August 2026. While there is some significant overlap between them, I nevertheless consider the most appropriate way to approach the costs of those applications is to order that they be costs in the cause.
